system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-07-12 18:10:00 to 2179-07-14 14:47:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old female with end-stage renal disease, diastolic heart failure, and atrial fibrillation was admitted for acute respiratory distress due to fluid overload from acute-on-chronic diastolic heart failure. She presented with severe hypertension and pulmonary edema, requiring emergent hemodialysis with removal of approximately 3 liters of fluid. A central line was placed in the left femoral vein due to difficult IV access, later removed without complication. Her symptoms improved rapidly post-dialysis, and she was weaned off respiratory support. A urinary tract infection with Enterococcus was identified and treated with levofloxacin, while infectious workup for pneumonia was negative. She remained hemodynamically stable with normal cardiac enzymes and was discharged home on her baseline medications with adjustments to warfarin dosing and instructions to complete a short course of antibiotics and monitor INR closely.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic heart failure
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having trouble breathing. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been short of breath for a few days, especially when I lie down. I had dialysis earlier this week, and I thought it was a full run, but I still feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re on dialysis three times a week, correct? And you’ve been taking all your medications as prescribed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every Monday, Wednesday, Friday. I haven’t missed any doses. I’ve also been careful with salt and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your records. You were just in the hospital a few weeks ago for similar symptoms. This time, your blood pressure was very high in the field—220 over 100—and you were breathing fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel that high. I didn’t even have a headache. But I couldn’t catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with fluid buildup. Your lungs were full of fluid—what we call pulmonary edema. It’s due to your heart not relaxing properly between beats, which is part of your diastolic heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my heart again? Not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. You’re not running a fever, and your chest X-ray doesn’t show pneumonia. It shows signs of heart failure—enlarged heart and fluid around the lungs. We think this is another flare-up due to fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I just had dialysis. How did I get overloaded?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes even a full dialysis session doesn’t remove enough fluid, or your blood pressure spikes and causes fluid to leak into the lungs. We’ll plan for dialysis tomorrow to remove the excess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. That makes sense. What about my blood pressure now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s much better—143 over 79 now. You’re on your usual meds: lisinopril, metoprolol, and valsartan. We’ll keep those going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been having more pain in my left eye. It’s been bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noted that. You’re already on eye drops. We’ll continue them and set up an outpatient appointment with your ophthalmologist to check it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m worried about my blood thinners too. I heard something about my INR being high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your INR was 4.1, which is too high. That means your blood is too thin, increasing your risk of bleeding. We’ve held your warfarin for two days and will restart it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that could happen. Should I stop it at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just this once. We’ll restart it the day after you go home. You’ll need to check your INR again soon after to make sure it’s in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my dialysis—when exactly will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning at 12:00. The team will come get you. After that, you should feel much better—less shortness of breath, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. I just want to get back home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still a bit winded, but not as bad as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs this morning show your kidney function is stable. Potassium was high but likely due to a hemolyzed sample. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe for me to have dialysis with high potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because dialysis will correct it. We’ll check it again after the session. Your heart enzymes are stable, so no sign of a heart attack—just strain from high blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on dialysis. How’s your breathing now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better! I can lie flat without gasping. I feel lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s exactly what we hoped for. Your blood pressure is staying in the 120s to 150s, which is good. Your INR dropped to 3.2, so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if everything stays stable. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll restart warfarin the day after, and get your INR checked in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No major changes. We switched your metoprolol from the long-acting to the regular one, twice a day. It’s easier to adjust. Everything else stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my diet and fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before: 2-gram sodium diet, and limit fluids to 1 liter per day. Weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And my eye appointment—I’ll follow up on that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ve reviewed your discharge instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I restart warfarin the day after today, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tomorrow morning. And get your INR checked within the next few days. Keep taking your other meds, watch your weight, salt, and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back to the ER. Same for chest pain, confusion, or any other new symptoms. You’ve been through this before—you know your body best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better and ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old female with end-stage renal disease and chronic diastolic heart failure was admitted for acute shortness of breath and severe hypertension, with initial presentation of pulmonary edema. She had recently undergone dialysis but developed fluid overload, leading to flash pulmonary edema. She was stabilized with blood pressure management and a session of hemodialysis, after which her respiratory symptoms resolved. Her INR was found to be supratherapeutic at 4.1, prompting a two-day hold on warfarin, with plans to restart post-discharge. She remained hemodynamically stable, with no evidence of infection or acute coronary syndrome. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to restart anticoagulation, monitor INR, adhere to fluid and sodium restrictions, and follow up with her specialists.
